title: Emor: one law (Leviticus 24:22)
hook: "Ye shall have one manner of law, as well for the stranger, as for the home-born"

segments.voice: Yesterday, Emor paused its feasts to remind the reapers to leave something for the poor. Your line was remember them at the feast. Today, the end of Emor, and a story about an outsider.

A fight in the camp. Near the end of Emor, the long list of laws suddenly breaks into a story. One of the men has an Israelite mother, Shelomith, daughter of Dibri, from the tribe of Dan, and an Egyptian father. In the quarrel, he curses the Name of God. Half-insider, half-outsider: does the law even apply to someone like him? Nobody is sure. They put him in custody and wait for an answer.
screen: `A FIGHT IN THE CAMP.` → `AN ISRAELITE MOTHER, AN EGYPTIAN FATHER.` → `DOES THE LAW APPLY TO HIM?`

segments.voice: The verdict comes, and it's severe, as the Torah's punishments for cursing God are. Then the text widens from this one man to everyone, with laws about harming people and animals. In the middle sits the answer to the question that started it all. In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "Ye shall have one manner of law, as well for the stranger, as for the home-born; for I am the LORD your God." The Hebrew word for stranger is ger, someone living among the people who wasn't born into them. The same law protects them and binds them: no special harshness for the outsider, no special leniency for the insider. It isn't the first time. At the very first Passover, in Exodus, the Torah already set down one law for the home-born and for the stranger who lives among you. Now, at a moment of real doubt, it says it again. The hard verse nearby gets the same treatment. This passage has the line people quote as an eye for an eye. The rabbis of the Talmud ruled that it means payment, the value of an eye, not an actual eye, and argued for it at length. Rabbinic law followed that ruling, and applied it, for the same injury, to everyone. One measure, for the ger and the home-born alike. And it started with a man nobody was sure about.
screen: `A STORY BREAKS INTO THE LAWS.` · `GER: THE ONE WHO LIVES AMONG YOU.` · `ONE LAW SINCE THE FIRST PASSOVER.` · `AN EYE MEANS ITS VALUE.` · then, large: `ONE LAW FOR ALL.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who's a stranger in a place you know well: the new person at work, the neighbor with an accent, the family that moved in last month. Notice whether you hold them to a different standard, stricter or more dismissive, than the people you grew up with. Then picture treating them by exactly the same rules as everyone else.
Emor. The portion that ends with one law for the stranger and the home-born alike.
Your line: one law for all. The outsider stands on the same ground as you. Day four hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: Jewish law and teaching repeatedly cite the Torah's command not to wrong the ger, the stranger, and the Passover seder's memory of being strangers in Egypt is often linked to welcoming outsiders.

chat.says: Does the Torah have a separate, harsher law for outsiders?
options: No. Leviticus says one law for the stranger and the home-born alike.
Yes. Outsiders were held to stricter rules than people born inside.
Yes, until the rabbis of the Talmud softened it centuries later.

notes: JPS 1917 Lev 24:22 quoted from memory, matching the index hook; confirm the ending '; for I am the LORD your God.'
The blasphemer's execution (24:14, 23) is described as 'severe' without detail, for the app's tone; a Keeper may prefer it named.
Exodus 12:49 (one law for the home-born and the stranger, at the Passover) paraphrased; confirm.
Bava Kamma 83b–84a: eye for an eye as monetary compensation. The script says courts following the rabbis never took eyes; confirm phrasing.
The ger in rabbinic law is often read as the convert (ger tzedek) or resident alien (ger toshav); the script uses the plain sense 'someone living among the people'.
